title: The turkey prince
hookLine: a prince thinks he's a turkey, and a sage sits under the table with him

lines: HELPING SOMEONE WHO WON'T BE HELPED.
A PRINCE WHO THINKS HE'S A TURKEY.
cards: Remember the last time you tried to help someone who didn't want help. A friend spiraling. A teenager who wouldn't talk.
A parent refusing to see the doctor. You stood over them with good advice, and the more right you were, the more they dug in.
Rebbe Nachman told a short, funny parable about exactly that: a royal family, a dining table, and a prince who has decided he is a turkey.
It's one of the most loved stories in the Breslov tradition, still retold in classrooms and therapy offices.

teach.b: A prince goes mad. He decides he's a turkey. He takes off his clothes, crawls under the table, and pecks at crumbs on the floor.
The king calls every doctor in the land. They argue with him, they order him, they try every cure. Nothing.
Then a wise man comes and says: let me try. He takes off his own clothes, crawls under the table, and starts pecking crumbs. The prince stares.

teach.h: THE WISE MAN: ALSO A TURKEY.
teach.b: A turkey, says the wise man. And you? Also a turkey.
So they sit together, two turkeys, and become friends. After a while, the wise man asks for a shirt. The prince is shocked.
Who says a turkey can't wear a shirt? You can wear a shirt and still be a turkey. So they both put on shirts.

teach.h: A SHIRT, THEN TROUSERS, THEN FOOD.
teach.b: Later, real food from the table: you can eat good food and still be a turkey. Then one day: you can sit at the table and still be a turkey. Little by little, the prince lives like a prince again.

The Yiddish word for turkey is hindik, and Breslov Hasidim still call this the hindik story. Teachers read it on more than one level. On the plain level, it's about how to help: don't shout from the chair.
Start where the other person is, and move one step at a time.
On a deeper level, many read it about the soul: nobody jumps from the floor to the table in one leap.

how: The turkey prince parable is retold in Breslov circles, Jewish schools and sermons, often as a lesson in patience and in meeting people where they are.

o: Hebrew for a wise man who acts the fool
Yiddish for turkey, the bird the prince thought he was
Yiddish for a fool who believes he's royalty

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.

s: the wise man cures the prince by arguing him out of it
he gets under the table and joins him first.
the prince starts wearing clothes while still calling himself a turkey
you can wear a shirt and still be a turkey, says the wise man.
the cure happens in one day
shirt, trousers, food, then the table: little by little.

games.q: you're the wise man. the prince is under the table, pecking crumbs, and every doctor has failed. what do you do?
o: explain firmly that he's a prince.
take off your clothes and sit under the table with him.
games.why: he joins the prince on the floor, becomes his friend, and brings him back one step at a time.

practice: Think of one person you've been trying to change, or fix, or talk sense into, and stop standing over them and get down to where they are.
What does the world look like from under their table, what are they afraid of, what would make them feel a little less alone?
Don't plan a speech; look for one small thing you could share, the way the wise man shared the floor, and if you pray, pray for them.

wordCard.voice: Hindik, Yiddish for turkey: Rebbe Nachman's parable of a wise man who got under the table with a prince who thought he was one.

carryVoice: Your line: sit under the table. The prince came back one shirt at a time. Day three hundred four, done.
